songs.title_en: The steppe, and steppe all around
songs.author: Ivan Zakharovich Surikov (1841–1880)
songs.published: first version 1869; revised 1877; folk-song version widely printed later
songs.source_detail: I. Z. Surikov, «В степи» («Кони мчат-несут…»), 1869/1877. Text: Wikisource, based on the Moshkov Library edition.
songs.rights_evidence: Surikov died in 1880; the poem was written in 1869 and revised in 1877. Public domain in Russia and the United States. The folk-song version is a traditional reworking and is not a modern arrangement.
translation: The horses race and carry me on,
By the way, do not forget
It is hard for me to leave her
Let her not grieve for me;
With the one her heart loves,
A groan stands in the steppe,
context: Surikov's poem was written in 1869 and revised in 1877. It became one of the most widely sung Russian songs about a death on the road: a coachman dying in the steppe gives his comrade instructions for burial, for the horses, for his parents and for his young wife. The poem does not name a province; the ‘Mozdok steppe’ locates it in the North Caucasus, on the road, not in a village.

The song is literary in origin, not a recorded folk lament. Its instructions — bury me here, take the horses home, tell my wife not to wait — are close to the formulas of a death on the road, but they are Surikov's composition. Use it as a literary song, not as a transcript of a peasant funeral.

notes.gloss: A coachman, a driver of a horse-drawn carriage or sled.
The steppe around Mozdok, in the North Caucasus; a named route, not a generic ‘Russian’ landscape.
Betrothal/wedding ring; the dying man returns it so that his wife is free to marry.

songs.title_en: From behind the island, into the reach
songs.author: Dmitrii Nikolaevich Sadovnikov (1847–1883)
songs.source_detail: D. N. Sadovnikov, «Из-за острова на стрежень…» (1883). Text: Wikisource, based on Poety-demokraty 1870–1880-kh godov (1968).
songs.rights_evidence: Sadovnikov died in 1883; the poem was published in 1883. Public domain in Russia and the United States. The folk-song version is a traditional reworking, not a modern arrangement.
translation: From behind the island, into the reach,
In the front boat Stenka Razin,
And the princess, lowering her eyes,
I will give my wild head!”—
Has traded us for a woman!
He spent a night with her—
By morning he has become a woman…
He has gone mad…” The mockery, the whisper
He embraces more tightly, her full waist;
His eyes filled angrily with blood,
So that there be no shame
With a mighty swing he lifts
“Why have you fallen silent, brave ones?..
For the repose of her soul!..”
context: Sadovnikov's poem was published in 1883 and became a folk song in the 1890s. It retells an episode from Kostomarov's study of Stenka Razin: the ataman throws his captive Persian princess into the Volga to stop his men's mockery. The last line is a command to sing ‘for the repose of her soul’ — a memorial formula used over a woman who has just been drowned.

The poem is literary, not a recorded song. It uses the river as a grave and the chorus as a memorial. It is relevant to the water plate and to the plates on the returning dead, but it is not evidence for a ritual. The ‘Persian princess’ is a literary figure; the poem gives no source for her.

notes.gloss: The deep, fast part of a river's channel.
Stepan Razin, the seventeenth-century Cossack leader of a major uprising; a figure of song and legend.
For the repose of the soul; a memorial formula, here used over a drowned woman.

songs.title_en: Along the wild steppes of Transbaikalia
songs.author: Anonymous (folk)
songs.source_detail: «По диким степям Забайкалья», no. 225 in Russkie narodnye pesni, zapisannye v Leningradskoi oblasti 1931–1949 gg., ed. V. A. Kravchinskaia and P. G. Shiriaeva (Leningrad–Moscow, 1950), p. 149. Text also in the 1908 songbook version on Wikisource.
songs.rights_evidence: A folk song published in lubok songbooks from 1908 to 1917; the text is traditional and public domain. The 1950 edition is a modern transcription; the atlas used the pre-1929 1908 version and the 1950 text only for collation.
original: В тюрьме он за правду страдал —
Бог знает, увижусь ли с ней!»
А брат твой давно уж в Сибири,
Пойдем же в курень наш родной,
translation: Along the wild steppes of Transbaikalia,
Where they dig gold in the mountains,
Dragged himself with a sack on his shoulders.
He walks through the dense taiga,
Where only the little birds sing,
Dry leather shoes beat his feet.
He fled from prison on a dark night,
In prison he suffered for the truth—
God knows whether I shall see her!”
His dear mother comes to meet him.
Is father well, I want to know?”
“Your father has long been in the grave,
And your brother has long been in Siberia,
Long has he rattled his chains.
Let us go, let us go, my son,
Let us go to our native hut,
Your wife there pines for her husband,
And the children weep in a crowd.”
context: A convict song known in many variants. The text printed here follows the pre-1929 songbook version; the 1950 Leningrad collection is cited for the song's later recorded form. The plot is a return: a man escapes across Baikal, meets his mother, and learns that his father is dead and his brother is in Siberia. The grave is not shown; it is reported in speech.

The song is relevant to the plates on roads, vanished villages and the empty house, but it is not a funeral text. It shows how the grave enters a family narrative at the moment of return. The ‘truth’ for which the prisoner suffered is a literary-political formula, not a documented charge.

notes.gloss: Transbaikalia, the region east of Lake Baikal.
A hut or cottage; in Siberian and Cossack usage, a home.
Penal servitude; the song's ‘prison’ and chains belong to that world.

songs.author: Anonymous (folk); literary source attributed to Nikolai Veryovkin, 1831
songs.date: literary source 1831; folk variant recorded later
songs.published: the Wikisource variant names no songbook; the literary source was published in 1831
songs.source_detail: «Чёрный ворон» (var. 1), Wikisource. The literary source is N. F. Veryovkin, «Под зелёною ракитой» (1831). The exact songbook of this variant is not named on the page.
songs.rights_evidence: The literary source was published in 1831 and its author died in the nineteenth century; the folk variant is traditional. Public domain. The exact songbook of this variant was not collated, so the edition is marked partial even though the text is public domain.
songs.verification: text public domain; edition not named
translation: Why do you circle above me?
You will not get your prey,
Black raven, I am not yours!
You will not get your prey,
Black raven, I am not yours!
Why do you spread your claws
Do you think to make me your prey?
Black raven, I am not yours!
Do you think to make me your prey?
Black raven, I am not yours!
In the midst of the fatal battle.
I see my death is coming—
Black raven, I am not yours!
I see my death is coming—
Black raven, I am all yours…
context: A Cossack song about a wounded man who answers the raven circling over him. The first three stanzas refuse the bird its prey; the last accepts it. The ‘marriage’ is to an arrow in battle, and the bloody handkerchief is to be carried to the beloved. The song is built on a single address and a reversal, not on a narrative.

The literary source is usually identified as Veryovkin's poem of 1831, but the text printed here is a folk variant. The Wikisource page names no songbook. Use it as a song text, not as a record of a specific funeral; the raven is an image of death, not a belief.

notes.gloss: A tempered arrow; ‘калёная’ means hardened by heat.
Dear love, sweetheart; a folk diminutive.
Married (in the church rite); here used metaphorically of the arrow that kills him.

songs.title_ru: Уж вы голуби, уж вы белые
songs.title_en: O you doves, you white doves (Verse on the Parting of Soul and Body)
songs.first_line: — Уж вы голуби, уж вы белые!
songs.author: Anonymous (traditional folk)
songs.published: P. A. Bessonov, Kaliki perekhozhie, vyp. 1 (Moscow, 1861)
songs.source_detail: P. A. Bessonov, Kaliki perekhozhie: sbornik stikhov i issledovanie, vyp. 1 (Moscow, 1861), stikh 17.
songs.rights_evidence: Bessonov died in 1898; the collection was published in 1861. Traditional folk text in the public domain in Russia and the United States.
original: — Уж вы голуби, уж вы белые!
— Мы не голуби, мы не белые,
Тебе, тело, в сыру землю идти,
В сыру землю идти, во сырой земле гнить,
А мне, душе, на суд праведный идти,
«Что ж ты, душа, мимо рая прошла,
Мимо рая прошла, в рай не зашла?
А у нас-то в раю жить весело,
translation: “We are not doves, we are not white doves,
How the soul parted from the body,
For you, body, it is to go into the damp earth,
To go into the damp earth, to rot in the damp earth,
And for me, the soul, it is to go to the righteous judgment,
To answer to Christ for my sins.’
They led the soul past Paradise.
‘Why, soul, have you passed by Paradise,
Passed by Paradise and not entered in?
For in Paradise it is joyful to live,
Singing the song of the seraphim:
Alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God!’”
context: A canonical Russian spiritual verse (dukhovnyi stikh), performed by wandering blind psalm-singers (kaliki perekhozhie) and village mourners at memorial meals, wakes, and church porches. The dialogue between the parting soul and guardian angels (appearing in the likeness of white doves) encapsulates the folk-theological drama of bodily decay versus spiritual trial.

In vernacular Orthodoxy, the body belongs irrevocably to the damp earth (syraia zemlia), while the soul embarks on an aerial transit past Paradise and the angelic realms to the divine judgment. Bessonov recorded numerous variants across central and northern provinces. In Plate H, this oral folk text stands beside the canonical liturgical sticheron, contrasting Church dogma with vernacular verse.

notes.gloss: Guardian angels; in vernacular belief, they escort the newly departed soul through the air to judgment.
Damp earth; the traditional poetic formula for the soil receiving the decomposing body.
The righteous or particular judgment (chastnyi sud) undergone by the individual soul after bodily death.
